lead: This unit explains how a small computer runs a petrol engine: how much fuel to inject, when to fire the spark, and how to keep the exhaust inside the legal limit. After it you can check a car against an emission stage, compute power, BMEP and BSFC from a test, size an injector pulse from manifold pressure, and set dwell and spark advance in crank degrees.
about: The unit follows one chain. Emission norms set the legal limits that force the whole exercise. Engine fuelling and exhaust emissions shows how the air-fuel ratio trades CO, HC and NOx, and why a three-way catalyst needs the mixture held at λ = 1. Torque, power and BSFC turn those choices into numbers a test cell measures. The concept of electronic engine control is the idea itself: open and closed loop, calibration maps and the block diagram of the engine management system. Electronic fuel control applies it to fuel (injectors, speed density, fuel trim), and ignition and spark timing control applies it to the spark (dwell, advance maps, knock control and misfire detection).

chapters.idea: An emission standard is a legal ceiling on pollutants per kilometre, and each new stage lowers that ceiling, so the engine must be controlled more precisely.
chapters.depth: Define the regulated pollutants: carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HC), oxides of nitrogen (NOx), particulate matter (PM) and particle number (PN). Explain that a limit is written in g/km and measured on a fixed driving cycle, so it describes the whole vehicle, not the engine alone. Trace the Euro ladder (Euro 1 to Euro 6) and its Indian copy, Bharat Stage I to VI. Note that India skipped BS V and moved from BS IV to BS VI in April 2020, and that sulphur in petrol fell from 50 ppm to 10 ppm with that fuel. Only a few universities teach this chapter; keep it short. Some syllabi call it 'emission legislation' or 'homologation limits'.

figure.title: From fuel to the legal limit
figure.aria: Fuel and air burn in the engine, the raw exhaust carries four pollutants into the catalyst, and only the tailpipe gas is compared with the legal limit.

chapters.example: A petrol car on the test cycle leaves 0.82 g/km CO, 0.07 g/km HC and 0.11 g/km NOx. Take the petrol passenger-car limits as BS IV: CO 1.0, HC 0.10, NOx 0.08 g/km; BS VI: CO 1.0, HC 0.10, NOx 0.06 g/km. (a) Does it pass BS IV? (b) Does it pass BS VI? (c) By what percentage does NOx exceed each limit? Answer: CO and HC pass both stages with 18 percent and 30 percent margin. NOx fails both: 0.03 g/km over BS IV, that is 37.5 percent high, and 0.05 g/km over BS VI, that is 83 percent high.
chapters.trap: Mixing the units. g/km is a vehicle limit from a chassis dynamometer; g/kWh is an engine limit from a steady test. A car can pass one and fail the other. Also, some stages set a combined HC + NOx limit, so you cannot compare them as two separate numbers.
chapters.leave: Driving-cycle details and the on-board diagnostics that check these limits in service to Unit 6; catalyst chemistry and the lambda sensor to 4.2 and Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Air-fuel ratio decides both what leaves the tailpipe and how much fuel the engine drinks, so the controller must pick a compromise at every operating point.
chapters.depth: Start from combustion: petrol needs about 14.7 kg of air per kg of fuel by mass (the stoichiometric ratio), and lambda λ is actual air-fuel ratio divided by 14.7, so λ < 1 is rich, λ > 1 is lean. Explain where each pollutant comes from: CO from rich mixture, HC from flame quench at the cold wall and from unburnt mixture, NOx from high flame temperature and long dwell at high temperature, PM from rich diesel spots. Show how the three pollutants move against λ. Cover the oxidising catalyst (burns CO and HC with air) and the three-way catalyst (also reduces NOx), its narrow window around λ = 1 and its light-off temperature near 250 to 350 °C. Explain exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) as dilution that lowers peak temperature and so NOx, at some cost in fuel. Finish with fuel economy: litre per 100 km, km per litre, and g CO2 per km.

figure.aria: CO and HC fall as the mixture goes lean while NOx rises to a peak just lean of lambda equal to one, so only a narrow band near lambda equal to one suits a three-way catalyst.

chapters.example: A car uses 6.8 L of petrol to cover 100 km. Petrol density is 0.74 kg/L and burning 1 kg of petrol makes about 3.16 kg of CO2. Find the fuel mass per 100 km, the mass per km, and the CO2 in g/km. Answer: 6.8 × 0.74 = 5.03 kg per 100 km, which is 0.0503 kg/km. CO2 = 0.0503 × 3.16 = 0.159 kg/km = 159 g/km. In the same car, when the air-fuel ratio drops to 13.2:1 under acceleration, λ = 13.2 ÷ 14.7 = 0.90, a rich power mixture that raises CO.
chapters.trap: Thinking a three-way catalyst cleans any mixture. Outside its window near λ = 1 one pollutant always runs away, so the catalyst is only as good as the fuel control loop feeding it. The second trap is forgetting that a cold catalyst does nothing: light-off matters, not just λ.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the limits, and the first-year chemistry of complete and incomplete combustion.
chapters.leave: Catalyst construction, the oxygen sensor and its voltage curve to Unit 3; how the map picks λ at each point to 4.4; closed-loop fuel trim to 4.5.

chapters.idea: Torque is what the engine twists with, power is torque times speed, and BSFC is how much fuel buys that power, so all three are needed to judge an engine.
chapters.depth: Define torque T in newton-metre and brake power P = 2πNT/60, with N in rev/min. Show why power keeps rising after torque peaks: speed wins. Define brake mean effective pressure only in one line as torque per unit swept volume. Define fuel flow in kg/h and brake specific fuel consumption BSFC = fuel flow ÷ brake power, in g/kWh. Link BSFC to brake thermal efficiency, η = 3600 ÷ (BSFC × CV) with BSFC in g/kWh and calorific value CV in MJ/kg. Mention indicated power, friction power and mechanical efficiency η_m = brake ÷ indicated. Explain what a BSFC map looks like and why the lowest island sits at moderate speed and high load. Only a few universities teach this chapter in depth.

figure.aria: Torque peaks at 3000 rpm and falls away, while power keeps climbing to about 69 kW at 6000 rpm because it is torque multiplied by speed.

chapters.example: A dynamometer holds an engine at 3000 rpm and measures 150 N·m; the fuel scale shows 11.5 kg/h of petrol. Petrol calorific value is 43 MJ/kg. Find brake power, BSFC and brake thermal efficiency. Answer: P = 2π × 3000 × 150 ÷ 60 = 47 124 W = 47.1 kW. BSFC = 11 500 g/h ÷ 47.1 kW = 244 g/kWh. η = 3600 ÷ (0.244 × 43) = 3600 ÷ 10.49 = 343, so 34.3 percent.
chapters.trap: Using rev/min directly in P = Tω. Convert first: ω = 2πN/60 rad/s. Second trap: BSFC is in g/kWh, so fuel flow must be in grams per hour before dividing, and the 3600 in the efficiency formula assumes exactly those units.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 for why a rich mixture that gives best torque also costs fuel, and basic physics of work, power and energy.
chapters.leave: Friction and pumping loss breakdown to a machine course; dynamometer operating procedure to the laboratory; the fuel map that stores these targets to 4.4.

chapters.idea: An electronic engine control unit reads sensors, looks up calibrated maps and drives actuators in a loop, holding the engine at the best compromise far more accurately than any mechanical device.
chapters.depth: Give the motivation first: a three-way catalyst needs λ held within about one percent over a whole life of wear and temperature, which no carburettor can do. Define open loop (output from maps alone, no feedback) and closed loop (output corrected by a measured result), with fuel control as the example. Explain calibration: a grid of engine speed against load, one stored value per cell, and linear interpolation between cells; the whole grid is the engine map. Draw the ECU block diagram: sensors, signal conditioning, analogue-to-digital conversion, processor with memory, driver stages, actuators. Describe control modes: cranking, warm-up enrichment, open-loop, closed-loop, deceleration fuel cut, idle control, limp-home. Name the two air-measurement methods, speed density and mass airflow, and say which chapter computes them.

figure.title: Engine management loop
figure.aria: Sensors such as manifold pressure, throttle, coolant and lambda feed conditioning circuits, the ECU looks up its maps and drives injectors, the coil and the EGR valve.

chapters.example: In the injection-duration map for a warm engine, the column for 2000 rpm holds 4.0 ms at 40 kPa manifold pressure and 6.0 ms at 50 kPa. The ECU reads 46 kPa. Find the pulse width, and the fraction of one engine cycle it takes. Answer: linear interpolation gives 4.0 + (6.0 − 4.0) × (46 − 40) ÷ (50 − 40) = 4.0 + 1.2 = 5.2 ms. At 2000 rpm one cycle of a four-stroke is 2 × 60 ÷ 2000 = 0.060 s = 60 ms, so the injector is open for 5.2 ÷ 60 = 8.7 percent of the cycle.
chapters.trap: Calling a map-based output 'closed loop'. A lookup from a table is open loop even though it is electronic; the loop closes only when a sensor measures the result and the ECU corrects for it. The second trap is interpolating along the wrong axis of the grid.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 to 4.3, so that the map targets mean something.
chapters.leave: Sensor construction and signal details to Unit 3; CAN bus, OBD-II and diagnostics to Unit 6; transmission and cruise control to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Electronic fuel control computes the air trapped in each cylinder, turns it into an injector open time, and trims that time from the exhaust oxygen sensor so the mixture stays at λ = 1.
chapters.depth: Show why the carburettor cannot meet the norm: fixed jets, no feedback, poor atomisation, bad behaviour on cold start and transients. Describe electronic carburetion (a feedback mixture solenoid on the carburettor) as the stop-gap, then petrol injection: throttle-body, port (PFI) and direct (GDI). Describe the solenoid injector, its static flow rating and the difference between saturated and peak-and-hold drives. Do the fuel chain: air mass from speed density, m_air = η_v × ρ × V_d × N ÷ 2, then fuel = air ÷ air-fuel ratio, then pulse width = fuel ÷ injector flow. Explain closed loop with the exhaust gas oxygen (EGO) sensor, short-term and long-term fuel trim, and the λ = 1 window. Cover the actuators: EGR valve driven by a stepper motor or a vacuum diaphragm and solenoid, idle air stepper motor, evaporative purge valve.

figure.title: Closed-loop fuel control
figure.aria: Air charge sets a base pulse from the map, the injector fires, the oxygen sensor measures lambda and the trim feeds a correction back into the base pulse.

chapters.example: A four-cylinder 1.6 L petrol engine runs at 3000 rpm with volumetric efficiency 0.85 and intake air density 1.16 kg/m3. Take the air-fuel ratio as 14.7:1 and an injector that flows 3.0 g/s when fully open. Find air flow, fuel flow, fuel per injection and injector open time. Answer: air per revolution = 1.6 L ÷ 2 = 0.8 L; at 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s the swept flow is 0.04 m3/s; actual air = 0.85 × 0.04 × 1.16 = 0.0394 kg/s = 39.4 g/s. Fuel = 39.4 ÷ 14.7 = 2.68 g/s. Each injector fires 3000 ÷ 2 ÷ 60 = 25 times a second, so 100 injections a second in all, giving 2.68 ÷ 100 = 26.8 mg per injection. Open time = 0.0268 ÷ 3.0 = 0.0089 s = 8.9 ms.
chapters.trap: Using engine displacement per revolution for a four-stroke. Only half the cylinders induct air per revolution, so divide the swept volume by two. The second trap is using manifold air density in the speed-density formula but the ambient figure in the example, or forgetting volumetric efficiency.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for open and closed loop, Unit 3 for the MAP, throttle and oxygen sensors and for stepper and solenoid actuators.
chapters.leave: Injector spray pattern and nozzle design to a mechanical course; diesel fuel injection to an elective; oxygen sensor voltage curve and heater circuit to Unit 3; fuel pump and wiring to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: The ECU sets spark timing from speed and load, charges the coil for a fixed time called dwell, and pulls timing back when the knock sensor complains.
chapters.depth: Recap the coil: current builds while the primary circuit is closed, and the stored energy ½LI² is released at the break. Define dwell time in ms and dwell angle in degrees; at constant dwell time the angle grows with speed because 1 ms equals N × 360 ÷ 60 000 degrees. Explain spark advance in degrees before top dead centre, minimum advance for best torque (MBT) and the knock limit that usually sits below it. Show the spark map versus speed and load, with corrections for coolant temperature, intake air temperature, EGR and knock. Describe closed-loop knock control: the knock sensor, the retard step and the slow advance back. Mention misfire detection from crank speed fluctuation. Programmed ignition, distributorless and direct coil-on-plug systems belong to Unit 2; here only the control side is needed.

figure.aria: Starting from the moment the coil begins to charge, the primary stays closed for 54 crank degrees, the spark falls at 54 degrees, and the burn runs on for another 56 degrees.

chapters.example: At 3000 rpm the ECU wants the spark 25 degrees before top dead centre and a dwell of 3.0 ms. (a) How many crank degrees is 3.0 ms at this speed? (b) At what angle must the coil start charging? (c) At 6000 rpm the coil needs only 2.0 ms: find the new dwell angle and start angle. Answer: 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s = 18 000 degrees/s, so 1 ms is 18 degrees. (a) 3.0 ms = 54 degrees. (b) The coil must close 54 degrees before the spark, so at 25 + 54 = 79 degrees before top dead centre. (c) At 6000 rpm, 1 ms is 36 degrees, so 2.0 ms = 72 degrees and charging starts at 25 + 72 = 97 degrees before top dead centre.
chapters.trap: Adding degrees to milliseconds, or taking dwell angle as constant. Dwell time is fixed by the coil and the current limit; dwell angle changes with speed. The second trap is calling the advance angle a time: it is a crank angle, so the same 25 degrees is half as many milliseconds at 6000 rpm as at 3000 rpm.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for maps and closed loop, 4.5 for the shared corrections, and Unit 2 for how the coil and spark plug work.
chapters.leave: Distributorless and direct ignition hardware, spark plug construction and heat range to Unit 2; knock sensor and crank sensor construction to Unit 3; misfire codes and OBD-II to Unit 6.
